newsitem.title: INDIA: India L&T says no plans to restructure further.
newsitem.headline: India L&T says no plans to restructure further.

text.p: India's largest engineering and construction firm Larsen and Toubro Ltd (L&T) has no plans to further restructure its businesses, managing director Sudhakar Kulkarni said.

In a recent tie-up with Japan's Komatsu Ltd, L&T spun off its earthmoving machinery division as a separate company, touching off speculation that this might be the first step in a series of spin-offs, analysts said.
But Kulkarni scotched the idea in a recent interview with Reuters, saying that was a step towards increasing competitiveness.

"This is not a hiving off, except in the sense that a business which was run as a part of the company, a department of the company, is being restructured into a separate company as a joint venture with somebody else," Kulkarni said.

"Today you have to look at each business separately and see what you need to do," he added. "You have to today worry very much about the competitiveness of the industry, because it is no more a closed protected market.
"It's an international business now. On your own turf it is international business, because these machines can really come from abroad and all that."

Kulkarni said L&T had come to the conclusion that there was considerable potential for the earthmoving machinery division to grow and expand, but its volumes were too small to justify an intensive independent research and development effort.
"If the infrastructure development takes place there will be need for construction equipment and this business even otherwise has been growing very fast," Kulkarni said.
India's infrastructure bottlenecks have begun to hamper the progress of its economic reforms. Analysts estimate the sector will require annual investments of over $30 billion upto 2000.
"The only problem is with our volumes -- we make 500 machines or so -- we cannot really afford to spend a lot of money on the development of machines."
Kulkarni said the Komatsu tie-up, with each partner holding equal shares, was essentially technology-driven.

"The consideration of technology is the consideration in this case," he added. "This is not an idea that we want to hive off all our businesses into separate companies, one by one, and do that sort of thing.
"This is an area where we felt that to be competitive in the long run, it was necessary for the company to have a technology tie-up."
Kulkarni said L&T had no plans to spin off other successful divisions, but he did not rule out the possibility of similar future tie-ups.
"If we come to the conclusion that there's another area where we need such a tie-up then it would be probably done. Each case will be examined separtely."

But rather different considerations had prompted L&T to spin off its information technology division as a separate company, Kulkarni said. L&T's reputation as an engineering firm had overshadowed the software division's performance.
"We have recently spun off our software development business as a separate company, a 100 percent subsidiary," he said.
"When it was part of L&T, L&T had an image as an engineering and construction company, so the outside world did not take our software activity very seriously."
The setting up of L&T Information Technology Ltd enabled L&T to structure the division along the lines of other successful infotech firms, sharpening focus and raising its profile.
"So it was for different considerations we decided to spin it off," Kulkarni said. "But we said we don't need a tie-up we will be a 100 percent subsidiary."
